title: Iowa: history overview
d: Iowa: the Hawkeye State, admitted 1846 (29th); capital Des Moines.
definition: Iowa: the Hawkeye State, admitted 1846 (29th); capital Des Moines.
description: Iowa — "Hawkeye State" — entered the Union 1846 (29th). Its capital is Des Moines and its largest city is Des Moines. Meskwaki and Sioux; Black Hawk War. This database tells the state's story: from its first peoples through statehood to the modern era, plus the famous sons and daughters, the industries, and the facts every resident should know.

title: Statehood
description: Iowa achieved statehood 1846 (29th). The road to statehood ran through territorial government, population thresholds, and a congressional enabling act — the standard American path. Corn and hogs; caucus fame. Statehood Day is still celebrated, and the admission order gives Iowa its number among the states.

title: The statehood story
d: How Iowa went from territory to state.
definition: How Iowa went from territory to state.
description: The statehood story of Iowa: settlement, territorial organization, the push for admission, and finally the star on the flag. Bridges of Madison County. Every state's admission reflected the national politics of its era — Iowa's story is no exception, and it explains much about the state's character today.

title: Capital: Des Moines
d: Des Moines is the capital of Iowa.
definition: Des Moines is the capital of Iowa.
description: Des Moines has been the seat of Iowa government, home to the capitol building, the supreme court, and the legislature. Capitals are often not the biggest city — Iowa's largest is Des Moines — chosen instead for geography or politics. Visit the capitol: the building itself tells the state's story in stone.

title: Nickname: Hawkeye State
description: The nickname "Hawkeye State" captures how Iowa sees itself — and how America sees it. The Iowa caucuses made it first-in-the-nation every four years. State nicknames come from history, geography, or industry, and they appear on license plates, tourism campaigns, and sports teams. The motto goes deeper: "Our liberties we prize and our rights we will maintain."
